1.translation: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Sañjaya, on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, my people and the sons of Pāṇḍu gathered, hungry for battle. What did they do?
1.nuances: Sivananda, Purohit and Adidevananda render dharmakṣetra as 'holy' or 'sacred' field, Prabhupada as 'place of pilgrimage', while Sankaranarayan keeps the literal 'field of righteousness' and adds a second, allegorical reading in which the two armies are selfish and wise intentions inside the human body. Gambirananda alone glosses māmakāḥ as 'my sons (and others)' rather than the broader 'my people'.

2.translation: Sañjaya said: When Duryodhana saw the army of the Pāṇḍavas drawn up in formation, the king went to his teacher and spoke these words.
2.nuances: Purohit and Sankaranarayan call Duryodhana 'prince' where the Sanskrit rājā and the other translators say 'king'. Most name the unnamed teacher as Droṇa in parentheses; Prabhupada adds an address 'O King' to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that is not in the verse.

3.translation: Teacher, look at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, marshalled by the son of Drupada, your own gifted pupil.
3.nuances: All agree on the sense; the differences are tonal. Purohit's 'Revered Father' for ācārya is an idiosyncratic choice, and Prabhupada adds 'so expertly arranged', sharpening the irony that Droṇa's student now leads the opposing force.

4.translation: Here are heroes and great bowmen, the equals of Bhīma and Arjuna in combat: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa and Drupada, a warrior of the first rank.
4.nuances: Mahāratha is handled variously: Sivananda's 'of the great car', Gambirananda's transliterated 'maharatha (great chariot-rider)', others simply 'mighty warrior' or 'great soldiers'. Sankaranarayan reads Virāṭa as 'the king of the Virata country' and Sivananda identifies Yuyudhāna as Satyaki.

5.translation: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna and the valiant king of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, a bull among men.
5.nuances: Purohit modernises Kāśī to 'Benares' and Gambirananda adds 'Varanasi'. Sankaranarayan drops Purujit as a proper name and reads it as an epithet of Kuntibhoja, 'the conqueror of many', while Purohit curiously attaches 'master over many' to Śaibya. Prabhupada paraphrases, discarding the narapuṃgava epithet.

6.translation: The valiant Yudhāmanyu and the mighty Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī: every one of them a great chariot-warrior.
6.nuances: The translators distribute the epithets vikrānta and vīryavān differently (Adidevananda swaps 'valiant' and 'strong' relative to Sivananda and Sankaranarayan). Purohit flattens mahārathāḥ to 'famous men'; Sivananda and Gambirananda identify Saubhadra as Abhimanyu.

7.translation: But now, best of the twice-born, take note of the most distinguished on our side, the commanders of my army. I name them so that you know them.
7.nuances: Dvijottama is 'best among the twice-born' for Sivananda and Sankaranarayan, 'best of Brahmanas' for Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada, and 'best of Spiritual Guides' for Purohit. Saṃjñārtham is read as 'for your information' by most, 'by way of example' by Gambirananda and 'to refresh your memory' by Adidevananda.

8.translation: Yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa and Kṛpa, victor in battle; Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa and the son of Somadatta as well.
8.nuances: Samitiñjaya is attached to Kṛpa by Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, but Prabhupada applies 'always victorious' to the whole list and Purohit to 'great soldiers' generally. Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan follow a variant text that adds Jayadratha (and Sankaranarayan also Śalya); Sivananda and Prabhupada identify Saumadatti as Bhūriśravā.

9.translation: And many other heroes, ready to lay down their lives for my sake, armed with all kinds of weapons, every one of them skilled in war.
9.nuances: All agree that these warriors are willing to die for Duryodhana. Gambirananda's 'dedicated their lives' and Sankaranarayan's present participle 'giving up their lives' are closer to tyaktajīvitāḥ than the softer 'ready to give up'; Prabhupada's 'experienced in military science' modernises yuddhaviśārada.

10.translation: That force of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, is inadequate; but this force of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is adequate.
10.nuances: This is the most disputed verse of the chapter: aparyāpta is 'insufficient' for Sivananda, Adidevananda and (in effect) Purohit, who hears Duryodhana's unease, but 'unlimited' or 'immeasurable' for Gambirananda and Prabhupada, who read it as a boast. Sankaranarayan prints both options and, following a different construal, swaps which army Bhīṣma and Bhīma protect.

11.translation: So let every one of you, standing firm at your posts in all the divisions, protect Bhīṣma above all.
11.nuances: Ayaneṣu is 'divisions' (Sivananda, Adidevananda), 'paths' (Sankaranarayan), 'positions in different directions' (Gambirananda) or 'points of entrance into the phalanx' (Prabhupada). Gambirananda alone preserves the honorific force of bhavantaḥ with 'venerable sirs', and Prabhupada again adds 'Grandfather' to Bhīṣma.

12.translation: Then, to lift Duryodhana's spirits, the mighty grandsire, eldest of the Kurus, let out a lion's roar and blew his conch.
12.nuances: All agree Bhīṣma blows the conch to cheer Duryodhana. Purohit alone merges the two sounds so the conch itself 'sounded like a lion's roar', while the rest keep the roar and the conch as separate acts; Sankaranarayan is characteristically literal with 'generating joy in him' and 'paternal grandfather'.

13.translation: At once conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and horns sounded all together, and the noise was tremendous.
13.nuances: The five instrument names are rendered loosely and inconsistently: gomukha becomes 'cow horns' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), 'blow horns' (Adidevananda) or just 'horns' (Purohit, Prabhupada), and Prabhupada introduces 'bugles'. Only Sivananda notes in parentheses that this is the Kaurava side.

14.translation: Then Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu, standing in their great chariot yoked with white horses, sounded their divine conches.
14.nuances: Prabhupada's 'transcendental conchshells' and 'Lord Kṛṣṇa', with the added 'On the other side', reflect his devotional framing; Purohit also writes 'Lord Shri Krishna'. Sivananda, Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan keep the epithet Mādhava and gloss it, whereas Adidevananda and Purohit substitute the names outright.

15.translation: Hṛṣīkeśa blew Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya blew Devadatta, and wolf-bellied Bhīma, doer of terrible deeds, blew his great conch Pauṇḍra.
15.nuances: Vṛkodara is kept as 'wolf-bellied' by Sivananda and Sankaranarayan, dropped by Purohit and Adidevananda, and turned by Prabhupada into 'the voracious eater'. Prabhupada also reads bhīmakarmā as 'performer of herculean tasks' and shifts 'terrific' onto the conch; Purohit alone calls Pauṇḍra 'renowned'.

16.translation: King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
16.nuances: The translators agree on the content; Purohit substitutes the title 'Dharmaraja' for Yudhiṣṭhira's name, and Prabhupada's 'The King of the Kunti's sons' is an awkward rendering of rājā kuntīputraḥ.

17.translation: The king of Kāśī, supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍī the great chariot-warrior; Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and Sātyaki the unconquered.
17.nuances: Purohit again uses 'Maharaja of Benares'. Prabhupada's version misplaces the epithets, making Kāśya a 'mighty car-warrior' and calling Śikhaṇḍī 'undefeated' as well as Sātyaki; the others keep parameṣvāsa with the king of Kāśī and aparājita with Sātyaki.

18.translation: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, lord of the earth, each blew his own conch.
18.nuances: Pṛthivīpate is a vocative to Dhṛtarāṣṭra for Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, but Prabhupada attaches 'King of the earth' to Drupada and Sankaranarayan omits it, instead glossing Drupada as 'the Pancala king' and noting Draupadī's sons are five. Adidevananda reads pṛthak pṛthak as 'again and again' rather than 'separately'.

19.translation: That roar, echoing through sky and earth, tore the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.
19.nuances: Dhārtarāṣṭrāṇām is 'sons of Dhritarashtra' for most but 'Dhritarashtra's party' (Sivananda) or 'men' (Sankaranarayan), reading it as the whole side. The verb vyadārayat ranges from 'rent' and 'pierced' to 'shattered'; Prabhupada expands the subject to 'the blowing of these different conchshells'.

20.translation: Then, seeing Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons in position as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pāṇḍu whose banner bears the monkey raised his bow, and spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa, lord of the earth.
20.nuances: Kapidhvaja is 'whose ensign was a monkey' (Sivananda, Sankaranarayan) but is identified as Hanumān by Purohit, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada. Pravṛtte śastrasampāte is read as weapons 'about to' fly (Sivananda, Gambirananda) or already 'beginning to fly' (Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan). Purohit and Adidevananda leave the sentence unfinished, carrying the speech verb into 1.21.

21.translation: Arjuna said: Acyuta, draw my chariot up between the two armies.
21.nuances: Several translators (Sivananda, Sankaranarayan, Prabhupada) merge 1.21 and 1.22 and add the purpose clause here. Acyuta is kept by Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan, rendered 'O Infallible' by Purohit and Prabhupada, and replaced by 'Krishna' in Sivananda and Adidevananda; Purohit mistakenly directs 'Lord of the earth' at Kṛṣṇa.

22.translation: Let me look at those who stand here eager for battle, and see whom I must fight in this great enterprise of war.
22.nuances: Purohit alone reads the verse as surveying both 'those who must fight on my side' and the enemy. Sankaranarayan's and Prabhupada's lines here actually belong to 1.23; Gambirananda renders raṇasamudyame as 'impending war', Adidevananda as 'enterprise of war'.

23.translation: I want to see those who have gathered here to fight, eager to do what pleases the ill-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
23.nuances: Durbuddhi is 'evil-minded' for Sivananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada, 'perverted' for Gambirananda and 'sinful' for Purohit, who also pluralises to 'sons'. Sivananda identifies the son as Duryodhana; Sankaranarayan's entry here is displaced from 1.24.

24.translation: Sañjaya said: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa brought the finest of chariots to a halt between the two armies.
24.nuances: Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan treat 1.24 and 1.25 as one unit. The vocative bhārata is given as 'O Dhritarashtra' (Sivananda, Adidevananda), 'descendant of Bharata' (Prabhupada, Sankaranarayan) or dropped (Purohit). Guḍākeśa is retained only by Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan; Purohit's 'bright chariot' is a free rendering of rathottama.

25.translation: There, before Bhīṣma and Droṇa and all the kings of the earth, he said: 'Pārtha, look at these Kurus assembled here.'
25.nuances: Purohit reads pramukhataḥ oddly as the place 'whither Bheeshma and Drona had led' the kings, while the rest take it as 'in front of'. Prabhupada's 'the Lord said' marks his devotional reading. Sankaranarayan's entry here is displaced from 1.26 and 1.27.

26.translation: There Pārtha saw standing fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends.
26.nuances: Gambirananda renders pitṝn as 'uncles' and brings 1.27's fathers-in-law and friends into this verse; Purohit adds 'cousins'. Sankaranarayan's line here is actually the second half of 1.27, which shows the differing verse divisions used by the sources.

27.translation: He saw fathers-in-law and well-wishers too, in both the armies. Looking at all these kinsmen drawn up there, the son of Kuntī
27.nuances: Suhṛdaḥ is 'friends' for most but 'benefactors' (Purohit) or 'well-wishers' (Prabhupada), distinguishing it from sakhīn in 1.26. Sivananda, Gambirananda and Prabhupada complete the sentence with the compassion clause from 1.28, while Purohit and Adidevananda leave it hanging as the Sanskrit does.

28.translation: was overcome by deep pity, and in despair he spoke. Arjuna said: Kṛṣṇa, seeing my own people here, gathered and spoiling for a fight,
28.nuances: Kṛpayā parayā is 'deep pity', 'supreme compassion' (Gambirananda) or 'his heart melted' (Purohit). Purohit replaces the vocative Kṛṣṇa with 'O my Lord' and Prabhupada with 'My dear Kṛṣṇa'. Gambirananda and Prabhupada already include the failing limbs of 1.29 here; Sankaranarayan's line is displaced from 1.30.

29.translation: my limbs give way and my mouth goes dry; my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
29.nuances: Mukham is 'mouth' for most but 'throat' for Purohit. Gambirananda's and Prabhupada's text here corresponds to 1.30 (Gāṇḍīva slipping, skin burning) and Sankaranarayan's to 1.31, so only Sivananda, Purohit and Adidevananda render this verse in place.

30.translation: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand and my skin is burning. I cannot stay on my feet, and my mind seems to spin.
30.nuances: Na śaknomy avasthātum is 'unable to stand' for Sivananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada but 'cannot keep quiet' for Purohit. Prabhupada paraphrases bhramatīva with 'I am forgetting myself'. Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada are displaced by one verse here.

31.translation: I see evil omens, Keśava, and I can see no good in killing my own people in battle.
31.nuances: Nimittāni viparītāni is 'adverse' or 'inauspicious omens' in all; Prabhupada (in his 1.30) expands Keśava into 'killer of the Keśī demon'. Purohit turns the second line into a rhetorical question. Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada are offset by a verse.

32.translation: I do not want victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor a kingdom, nor pleasures. What use is a kingdom to us, Govinda, what use are enjoyments, or life itself?
32.nuances: Sivananda replaces Govinda with 'Krishna', Purohit with 'my Lord'; Gambirananda and Prabhupada keep it. Gambirananda reads jīvitena as 'livelihood' rather than 'life' and merges 1.32 to 1.34 into one rendering. Purohit alone uses the singular 'I crave' and 'to me'.

33.translation: Those for whose sake we wanted a kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures stand here in battle, staking their lives and their wealth.
33.nuances: Prāṇāṃs tyaktvā is 'having renounced' (Sivananda, Adidevananda), 'about to sacrifice' (Purohit) or 'risking' (Gambirananda). Prabhupada's fragment omits the staking of life and wealth; Sankaranarayan's line is displaced from 1.34.

34.translation: Teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other kin.
34.nuances: The lists match closely; Purohit alone loses the distinction between maternal uncles (mātula) and generic 'uncles'. Prabhupada runs the verse into 1.35 and adds the vocative Madhusūdana here; Sankaranarayan's entry belongs to 1.35.

35.translation: I do not want to kill them, Madhusūdana, even if they kill me, not even for sovereignty over the three worlds, let alone for the earth.
35.nuances: Ghnato 'pi is 'though they kill me' for Sivananda, Adidevananda and Gambirananda; Purohit detaches it as 'It matters not if I myself am killed'. Prabhupada glosses Madhusūdana as 'maintainer of all living entities', an unusual etymology, and Sankaranarayan renders it 'slayer of Madhu'.

36.translation: What joy could we have, Janārdana, in killing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? Only sin would cling to us if we killed these aggressors.
36.nuances: Ātatāyinaḥ is the crux: 'felons' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'murderous felons' (Adidevananda), 'desperate men' or 'desperadoes' (Purohit, Sankaranarayan) and 'aggressors' (Prabhupada), the last reflecting the legal sense that killing an ātatāyin is normally permitted. Prabhupada's 'husband of the goddess of fortune' is his expansion of Mādhava from 1.37.

37.translation: So it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen. How could we ever be happy, Mādhava, after killing our own people?
37.nuances: Nārhāḥ is 'should not' (Sivananda), 'not proper' (Gambirananda), 'not befitting' (Adidevananda); Purohit turns it into 'we are worthy of a nobler feat'. Prabhupada's text here is shifted ahead to 1.38 and Sankaranarayan's only covers the second line.

38.translation: Even if they, their minds eaten away by greed, see no wrong in the destruction of a family and no crime in betraying friends,
38.nuances: Mitradrohe is 'hostility to friends' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'treachery to friends' (Adidevananda) or 'cheating friends' (Sankaranarayan). Lobhopahatacetasaḥ ranges from 'blinded by greed' (Purohit) to 'hearts perverted by greed' (Gambirananda). Gambirananda and Prabhupada fuse 1.38 and 1.39.

39.translation: how can we, Janārdana, who clearly see the wrong in destroying a family, fail to know that we must turn back from this sin?
39.nuances: Most read kathaṃ na jñeyam as 'why should we not learn to turn away'; Gambirananda's 'remain unaware of the need of abstaining' is the most literal, and Purohit's 'whose eyes are open' is the freest. Prabhupada's text here is actually 1.40.

40.translation: When a family is destroyed, its age-old family laws perish; when the law perishes, lawlessness overwhelms the whole family.
40.nuances: Kuladharmāḥ sanātanāḥ is 'immemorial religious rites' (Sivananda), 'traditional rites and duties' (Gambirananda), 'ancient traditions' (Adidevananda, Purohit) or 'eternal duties' (Sankaranarayan). Adharma becomes 'impiety', 'vice', 'irreligion' or 'lawlessness' depending on whether the translator hears a religious or a social breakdown.

41.translation: When lawlessness prevails, Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted; and when women are corrupted, Vārṣṇeya, the mixing of social orders follows.
41.nuances: Varṇasaṅkara is 'intermingling of castes' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), 'intermixture of classes' (Adidevananda) or 'adulteration of the stock' (Purohit); Prabhupada (whose text is displaced) speaks of 'unwanted progeny'. Purohit drops both vocatives.

42.translation: Such mixing leads to hell both for those who destroy a family and for the family itself, for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
42.nuances: Piṇḍodaka is rendered concretely as 'rice-ball and water' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), generically as 'ritual offerings of food and water' (Adidevananda) or as 'funeral cakes and ablutions' (Purohit). Purohit's 'promiscuity' is an unusually strong reading of saṅkara; Prabhupada's line here belongs to 1.43.

43.translation: Through these wrongs of the family-destroyers, which produce the mixing of social orders, the everlasting laws of caste and family are wiped out.
43.nuances: Jātidharma is 'rites of the caste' (Sivananda), 'duties of the castes' (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan) or 'class traditions' (Adidevananda, Purohit), the English word chosen reflecting each translator's comfort with 'caste'. Prabhupada's entry here is 1.44.

44.translation: Janārdana, we have heard that for men whose family laws have been wiped out, a dwelling in hell is certain.
44.nuances: Niyatam is 'inevitable' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'ordained' (Adidevananda) or 'certain' (Sankaranarayan); Sivananda alone adds 'for an unknown period', hinting at the variant reading aniyatam. Purohit paraphrases hell away as 'forever lost' and anuśuśruma as 'the wise say'; Prabhupada's text is 1.45.

45.translation: Oh, what a great sin we have resolved to commit: out of greed for the pleasures of kingship we are ready to kill our own people.
45.nuances: All agree on the sense; Purohit's 'countrymen' for svajanam is broader than the others' 'kinsmen' or 'kith and kin', and Adidevananda softens lobha to 'desire'. Prabhupada's text here belongs to 1.46.

46.translation: It would be better for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and unresisting.
46.nuances: Kṣemataram is 'better for me' (Sivananda, Adidevananda), 'better for my welfare' (Purohit) or 'more beneficial' (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan). Sankaranarayan reads dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ as 'Dhritarashtra's men' rather than his sons; Prabhupada's entry here is 1.47.

47.translation: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow and arrows and sank down onto the seat of the chariot, his mind shaken with grief.
47.nuances: Saṅkhye is 'in the midst of the battlefield' for most but Sankaranarayan construes it with the speech, 'having said this much about the battle'. Rathopastha is 'seat of the chariot' (Sivananda, Purohit, Adidevananda) or 'back of the chariot' (Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada's version of this verse appears under 1.46.

48.translation: Oṁ, that is the truth. Thus ends the first chapter, called the Yoga of Arjuna's Despair, in the Upaniṣads of the glorious Bhagavad Gītā, the science of Brahman, the treatise on yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
